Žiak môže vykonať ústnu formu internej č: Students may take the oral form of the internal part of the school-leaving examination regardless of their results in the external part and the written form of the internal part. The overall assessment takes into account both the oral and written results. If a student receives grade 3 or better in the oral examination, passing the entire school-leaving examination requires more than 25% of the total points in the written form of the internal part or more than 33% of the total points in the external part. If the oral grade is 4, the student passes only if they obtain more than 25% of the points in the written form of the internal part and, at the same time, more than 33% in the external part. A student who fails the oral examination may register for a resit, traditionally held during the additional examination period in September or February of the following year. The exact date is set by the school principal. This also applies to the theoretical part of the specialist component.

Vtedajšia úroveň školy vytvorila predpok: The school’s standard at the time made it possible to establish a teacher-training department alongside the music school on 10 October 1951. In 1954, this department became independent; three years later it was renamed the Higher Music School, and in 1961 it became the Conservatoire, training professional musicians for Žilina’s artistic and educational life. From 1955, the school was based in the Baroque Franciscan monastery. In the teacher-training department’s first year, only violin (L. Árvay) and piano (his wife, I. Árvayová) were taught, alongside music theory subjects. Interest in study gradually increased. The five-year programme became a six-year programme, and the most talented students could proceed to higher education after the school-leaving examination in Year 4. Student and teacher numbers continued to grow. Additional principal subjects were introduced: 1955 – clarinet, accordion and conducting; 1953 – cello and trumpet; 1955 – flute; 1957 – solo singing; 1960 – cimbalom; 1962 – oboe and French horn; 1963 – double bass, bassoon and trombone; 1966 – percussion; 1967 – viola; 1970 – guitar; 1972 – harp; 1994 – saxophone; and 1995 – organ. Composition and conducting are also taught, with church music offered since 1996. In 1994, the conservatoire gained a new building designed by architect Viery Meckovej, which significantly changed how the school operated. It provided generous, impressive facilities: a 250-seat concert hall, a movement studio, an organ classroom equipped with a pipe organ, space for the school library and suitable offices. In 2005, the conservatoire left the Baroque Franciscan monastery permanently and moved into the newly completed Building B. Principals of the Conservatoire: 1951 - 1958 Ladislav Árvay; 1958 - 1979 Vojtech Jakubík; 1979 - 1990 Milan Seidl; 1990 - 1995 Klára Cenková, née Kauzálová; 1995 - 2004 Ján Glasnák; 2004 - 2024 Milan Oravec; 2025 - present Zuzana Priečinská, née Šupková. The school celebrated its 70th anniversary in 2021. Its graduates have consistently ranked among Slovakia’s leading artists and teachers, and many have also enjoyed successful careers abroad. Notable graduates include: Tadeáš Salva, Igor Dibák, Pavol Krška, Vladimír Martinka, Lukáš Borzík – composition; Gabriela Beňačková, Ľubica Rybárska, Pavol Bršlík, Sisa Sklovská, Marián Vojtko, Andrea Danková, Martina Masaryková, Monika Fabiánová, Ivan Zvarík, Mária Porubčinová – voice; Bohumil Urban, Jindřich Pazdera, Miloš Valent, Stano Palúch, Dalibor Karvay – violin; Roman Patkoló – double bass; Pavol Tužinský, Štefan Sedlický, Karol Kevický, Adam Sedlický, Ján Goliáš (French horn) – conducting; Ján Labant, Miloš Slobodník, Adam Marec, Karol Samuelčík – guitar; Katarína Turnerová – harp; Ivan Gajan, Daniel Buranovský, Eva Varhaníková, Matej Árendárik, Róbert Pechanec, Peter Pažický, Aleš Solárik – piano; Boris Lenko – accordion; Pavol Valášek – organ; Igor Fábera – oboe; Albert Hrubovčák – trombone; Marek Pastírik, Miloslav Suchomel and Radovan Tariška – saxophone; Lukáš Oravec – trumpet. The largest group of graduates works at elementary arts schools, fulfilling the conservatoire’s most important mission: training music teachers for elementary music education.
